title: Hessdalen Lights
subtitle: Hessdalen valley · Norway, 1981
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, a remote snowy valley in rural central Norway at night in the early 1980s, dark spruce forest and low mountain ridges, a few scattered farmhouses, cold blue-grey light, melancholy and uncanny, cinematic wide composition, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: From December nineteen eighty-one, people in the Hessdalen valley, in central Norway, reported lights in the sky. Up to twenty times a week.
beats.img: A wide view down a dark snowy valley at night, a single small farmhouse window lit far below, low mountain ridges against an overcast sky, still and silent.

beats.vo: White, yellow, or red. Some hovered in mid-air for more than an hour. Others moved off at enormous speed.
beats.img: A single small bright white-yellow ball of light hovering in mid-air above a dark snowy valley floor at night, faint glow on the snow below, dark spruce trees, eerie stillness.

beats.vo: In nineteen eighty-three, researchers came to watch the valley, with cameras, and radar.
beats.img: A small field research hut on a snowy hillside at night with a tripod-mounted camera and a small radar antenna dish pointed at the dark valley, a dim lamp glowing inside, no people.

beats.vo: Since nineteen ninety-eight, an automatic station has watched the sky there, day and night.
beats.img: A small weatherproof automatic monitoring station box with cameras and sensors mounted on a pole on a snowy ridge above a dark valley at dusk, a faint red indicator light.

beats.vo: Proposed explanations include burning dust, and rock under strain. More than forty years on, there is no agreed explanation.
beats.img: An empty snowy valley at night under a vast dark sky, a faint distant point of light low over the ridge, cold and unresolved.

facts.claim: Peak activity Dec 1981–mid-1984, lights seen 15–20 times per week in the Hessdalen valley, rural central Norway
Colors bright white, yellow or red; hover in mid-air; duration a few seconds to well over an hour; sometimes move with enormous speed
Project Hessdalen began 1983; field investigations 1983–85 used cameras and radar (1984 radar detections)
Automatic measurement station installed 1998, monitoring the sky continuously
Hypotheses include combustion of dust and piezoelectricity (quartz under strain); no consensus explanation
